concepts.name: Origins and Economic Context of the Tebhaga Movement
key_dimensions: Exploitative sharecropping system: the 'adhi' (half-share) system and landlord dominance
Impact of the 1943 Bengal Famine as a precipitating economic grievance
Post-war agrarian distress, inflation, and the collapse of peasant livelihoods
Distinction between Tebhaga's economic roots vs. purely political anti-colonial movements

concepts.name: The Tebhaga Demand: Two-Thirds Share Formula
key_dimensions: Exact demand: shift from 50% (adhi) to 66.6% (two-thirds) share for sharecroppers (bargadars)
Who would hold the threshing floor — peasants vs. landlords — as the symbolic flashpoint
Comparison with demands of other peasant movements (Deccan Riots, Mappila rebellion) on revenue sharing
Why the two-thirds formula was considered radical yet economically justified

concepts.name: Role of the Bengal Provincial Kisan Sabha (BPKS)
key_dimensions: BPKS as the organizational backbone under the Communist Party of India (CPI)
How BPKS mobilized and coordinated across districts within weeks (Nov–Dec 1946)
Relationship between BPKS and the broader All India Kisan Sabha (AIKS)
Debate on whether party-led peasant movements distort or amplify grassroots agency

concepts.name: Role of the Communist Party of India (CPI) and Left Politics
key_dimensions: CPI's strategic decision to launch Tebhaga as a mass movement in the interim government period
Tension between CPI's support for the Congress-led independence movement and its class-struggle agenda
CPI's 'People's War' policy reversal and how it affected peasant mobilization post-1942
UPSC trap: Tebhaga was NOT a Congress-led movement; contrast with Congress-affiliated peasant agitations

concepts.name: Timeline and Geographic Spread of the Movement
key_dimensions: Launch: December 1946 — rapid spread across northern and eastern Bengal districts
Key districts: Dinajpur, Rangpur, Jalpaiguri, Midnapore, Murshidabad, and 24 Parganas
Peak mobilization: approximately 6 million peasants within weeks — scale vs. other movements
Decline by March 1947 due to state repression — compressed but intense timeline

concepts.name: Leadership and Key Figures of the Tebhaga Movement
key_dimensions: Banchharam Das, Bhowani Sen, and other CPI/BPKS leaders as primary organizers
Role of Sunil Sen (historian) in documenting the movement — source-critical angle for UPSC
Decentralized vs. centralized leadership: district-level autonomy within the BPKS framework
UPSC trap: Avoid confusing Tebhaga leadership with Telangana (Ravi Narayan Reddy) or Tebhaga with Terai movements

concepts.name: Extraordinary Participation of Women in the Tebhaga Movement
key_dimensions: Women peasants (including widows and lower-caste women) as frontline participants, not mere supporters
Nari Bahinis (women's brigades) formed under BPKS to lead marches and confront landlords
Intersection of class and gender: women's grievances beyond land — sexual exploitation by zamindars
Comparison with women's roles in other agrarian movements (Telangana, Champaran) — Tebhaga as exceptional

concepts.name: Caste and Class Dynamics in the Tebhaga Movement
key_dimensions: Predominance of low-caste and Dalit sharecroppers (e.g., Rajbanshis, Namasudras) as participants
Whether Tebhaga transcended caste identities or reinforced them through class-based mobilization
Role of the Scheduled Caste Federation vs. CPI in competing for lower-caste peasant loyalty
Contrast with the Mappila Rebellion where religion complicated class solidarity

concepts.name: Adivasi (Tribal) Participation in the Tebhaga Movement
key_dimensions: Santhals, Oraons, and other tribal sharecroppers in Dinajpur and Jalpaiguri as key participants
Overlap between Tebhaga and tribal forest rights demands — agrarian vs. forest movement distinction
How tribal participation distinguished Tebhaga from purely 'peasant' uprisings
UPSC trap: Tebhaga was not a tribal movement per se; tribals participated within a broader class framework

concepts.name: State Repression and the Role of the Provincial Government
key_dimensions: Bengal Congress government under H.S. Suhrawardy (Muslim League) deploying police and military
Section 144 imposed across districts; arrests of BPKS leaders including women activists
Contrast: repression by an Indian-led (pre-independence) provincial government vs. British colonial state
How state violence paradoxically strengthened short-term movement solidarity

concepts.name: Non-Violent Tactics and Peasant Strategies
key_dimensions: Primary tactic: physically occupying the threshing floor (khalaan) to enforce the two-thirds share
Use of lathis (bamboo staves), processions, and social boycott of landlords
Largely non-violent character of Tebhaga vs. violent episodes in Telangana — UPSC comparison trap
How 'direct action' methods differed from Gandhian satyagraha in agrarian context

concepts.name: Outcomes and the Bengal Bargadars Temporary Regulation Act (1947)
key_dimensions: Act of 1947: temporary legal recognition of two-thirds share — partial victory for peasants
Limitations: 'temporary' nature, no security of tenure, no abolition of zamindari
Later legislative follow-up: West Bengal Bargadars Act 1953 and Operation Barga (1978) as legacy
UPSC trap: Tebhaga did not achieve full demands; the 1947 Act was a compromise, not a triumph

concepts.name: Tebhaga vs. Telangana Movement: Comparative Analysis
key_dimensions: Both CPI-led; Tebhaga (1946–47) vs. Telangana (1946–51) — overlapping timelines
Tebhaga: non-violent sharecropping dispute; Telangana: armed guerrilla struggle against Nizam's feudalism
Geographic scope: Tebhaga confined to Bengal; Telangana covered three districts of Hyderabad state
Outcomes: Tebhaga achieved limited legal reform; Telangana was militarily suppressed after police action

concepts.name: Tebhaga Movement and the Independence Transition (1946–47 Context)
key_dimensions: Movement occurred during the critical interim government period — deliberate timing by CPI
How the movement complicated Congress's political consolidation before partition
Bengal's partition (1947) and its impact on the unfinished agenda of Tebhaga bargadars
Whether the independence moment helped or hindered peasant movement demands — a recurring UPSC theme

concepts.name: Historiography of the Tebhaga Movement: Subaltern vs. Nationalist Perspectives
key_dimensions: Subaltern Studies approach (Partha Chatterjee, Ranajit Guha): agency of peasants beyond party direction
Marxist historiography: Tebhaga as a textbook class struggle and CPI organizational success
Nationalist historiography's relative silence on Tebhaga — why it is underrepresented in mainstream narratives
UPSC angle: understanding historiographical bias helps answer 'critically examine' type questions

concepts.name: Zamindari System and Landlord Response to Tebhaga
key_dimensions: Landlord counter-mobilization: formation of armed lathial bands (private militias) to evict peasants
Role of Muslim League-affiliated zamindars in some districts — communal overlay on class conflict
How zamindars used legal instruments (eviction orders, false cases) alongside physical coercion
Connection to the eventual Zamindari Abolition Acts post-1950 as a systemic response

concepts.name: Long-term Legacy: Operation Barga and Land Reforms in West Bengal
key_dimensions: Operation Barga (1978–81): Left Front government's registration of bargadars — direct ideological heir to Tebhaga
How Tebhaga's unfinished demands shaped West Bengal's distinct land reform trajectory
Comparison with land reforms in other states (Kerala's land ceiling acts) — Bengal's unique path
Limits of land reform: Operation Barga gave security of tenure but did not redistribute land ownership

concepts.name: Tebhaga Movement and the All India Kisan Sabha (AIKS) Framework
key_dimensions: AIKS founded 1936 — role in providing ideological and organizational scaffolding for Tebhaga
How AIKS coordinated Tebhaga with simultaneous peasant agitations in Punjab and UP
Debate within AIKS: revolutionary land reform vs. immediate economic demands — which path for Tebhaga?
UPSC trap: AIKS ≠ Congress Kisan organization; it was CPI-affiliated and independent of the INC

concepts.name: Ecological and Agrarian Structure of Bengal as Context for Tebhaga
key_dimensions: Bengal's jute economy: sharecroppers growing jute for export market — global commodity linkage
Permanent Settlement (1793) legacy: absentee zamindars, multiple layers of intermediaries (jotedars, mahajans)
How the jotedar (rich peasant) class complicated the simple landlord-peasant binary in Bengal
UPSC trap: in Bengal, the intermediate jotedar class (not just zamindars) was the immediate exploiter of bargadars

concepts.name: Tebhaga, Civil Disobedience Traditions, and Peasant Consciousness
key_dimensions: Whether Tebhaga represented a new 'class consciousness' or continuation of traditional agrarian protest
Role of literacy campaigns and peasant schools (kisan pathshalas) by BPKS in raising political awareness
How the 1943 famine created a 'moral economy' rupture that radicalized previously passive sharecroppers
E.P. Thompson's 'moral economy' concept applied to Tebhaga — a common analytical lens in UPSC Mains essays
